traps.why: The ester does not stay in one piece. After the first hydride adds, ethoxide is expelled from the tetrahedral intermediate, so the OEt can never end up bonded to the benzylic carbon as an ether.
A single hydride does not give a stable hemiacetal. The tetrahedral intermediate expels ethoxide to give benzaldehyde, which LiAlH₄ reduces again.
Right idea to split the ester, but LiAlH₄ never stops at the aldehyde: benzaldehyde is more reactive than the ester and is reduced to benzyl alcohol straight away.
The route stops at the anion (alkoxide / phenoxide / thiolate / carboxylate): it never adds water or acid to protonate it.

explanation: Two hydrides add to the acyl carbon: the first gives a tetrahedral intermediate that expels ethoxide (benzaldehyde + ethoxide), the second reduces the aldehyde. After the H₂O step you hold benzyl alcohol AND ethanol.
tip: An ester always falls apart under LiAlH₄: count two alcohols on your clipboard.

traps.why: A lactone is a cyclic ester, not a cyclic ether. The C–O bond of the ester is broken on reduction; THF would need the ring to survive intact.
The hydroxy aldehyde is reduced on the spot by the excess hydride.
The cyclic hemiacetal is only an intermediate: it opens to the hydroxy aldehyde, which is reduced.
The route stops at the anion (alkoxide / phenoxide / thiolate / carboxylate): it never adds water or acid to protonate it.

explanation: The lactone is an ester whose two halves are tied together, so the 'two alcohols' end up in one molecule: butane-1,4-diol.
tip: Cyclic ester → one diol. The two OH groups are the two ester oxygens' fates.
